paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, well this is my last podcast to you before I'm released later today. I wanted to share a few stories that I think might help you remember some of the key principles that I've tried to teach you about life during and after the mission. At the beginning of my mission, Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve spoke privately with me and said this: "Make sure you teach your missionaries how to succeed in life. They need to know that their mission is just the beginning and should not be the biggest success they ever have." He then repeated himself by saying, "Teach them how to succeed in life." I've tried to keep that promise and that counsel with you and with all the other missionaries that we have served with during our three years here in the Quezon City North Mission. I hope some of those teachings have found a place in your map or your mindset and will help you guide your life in such a way that you'll find success in achieving your most important and righteous goals.

The first lesson is to never give up on a worthy goal. The story is in the Western United States, and this is a true story by the way, during the 1800s there were large deposits of gold that were discovered in the mountains. This discovery set off a huge gold rush. Many men and their families sold all their property in the eastern United States and made their very difficult trek out west to seek their fortune. One man sold all that he had to buy a mining claim in Colorado. He worked hard for very many months digging and digging and digging, but he just didn't find very much gold. He finally got so discouraged that he sold his claim to another miner for less than he paid for it before he had done all the work. The new man wisely hired a mining engineer to survey the mine. The engineer did the necessary research and found that there was a very large vein of gold only three feet away from where the first miner had stopped digging.

Elders and sisters, remember that when things start to get hard, always, always try to persevere through that adversity. Most of the rewards in life come after the storm. Most of the rewards in life come in the second mile or the second kilometer. These cliches are cliches for a reason, and that is that they're so often true. But unfortunately, many people give up on following their dreams because the work becomes too difficult, or takes too long, or it's too tedious or boring. But often you're closer to the finish line than you may think, and if you'll push just a little harder or just a little longer, you'll actually succeed. We all must remember that good things don't come easily, and if we give up too soon or don't do the proper research, those good things actually never come to us. So never give up on a worthy goal.

The second lesson is to invest your time wisely. A professor once stood up before his class with a large, empty glass jar. While his students watched, he filled the glass jar to the top with large rocks and then asked his students if the jar was full. His students all agreed that the jar was full. The professor then said, "No, there is still more room in the jar," and he then added a large amount of very small pebbles to the jar, gave the jar a little bit of a shake, and the pebbles all dropped in to fill in the cracks among the larger rocks. Then he asked the class again, "Is the jar full now?" The students said that now the jar really was full, but the professor disagreed again and said there's still plenty of room.

He then took a large amount of sand and poured the sand into the jar. The sand then filled in all the remaining little empty spaces between the large and the small rocks. Now all agreed that the glass jar was completely full. Your life is like the jar, and the rocks, the pebbles, and the sand are like the projects and activities you choose to do in your life.

The rocks represent the most important projects, such as spending time with your family, building a great work life, maintaining good health, and serving the Lord and your fellow man. The pebbles represent the things in your life that matter, but that you could actually live without if you had to. They are maybe sort of important, but they're not essential. The pebbles are certainly things that give your life some happiness, maybe like hobbies and friendships, but they're not critical to you to have a meaningful, powerful life. These things often come and go and are not permanent or essential to your overall well-being, even though they may feel like it at the time. Finally, the sand represents the remaining things in your life. This could be small things such as watching television or browsing through your favorite social media site. These things don't really mean very much to your life and, frankly, they're generally things you just do to waste time or to get small things accomplished.

The key lesson is that if you don't plan well and discipline yourself, you will probably start out many days by putting pebbles, or worse yet, putting sand in your jar. And then you will not have room for the rocks—the really big, important, and life-sustaining projects that are so valuable to a significant life. This holds true with the things you let into your life from the outside and the things that you choose to do from your own free will and choice. If you spend all of your time on the small and insignificant things, you will run out of room for the things that are actually important.

This, one of these sort of things, happened to me this very morning where someone asked me to do something for them. And it was a good thing, but if I'd said yes to that request, I would have had to say no to some very important things that I had to do for you and for the mission today. And so I regretfully and politely said no, I just couldn't do that thing right now, because to do that would take away from previous and frankly more important commitments that I had made. You have to learn how to say no to others and most importantly to yourself before you can learn how to say yes to those most important things in your life. So in order to have a very effective and rewarding life, know what the rocks are for you and pay attention to them and do them first because they are critical to your long-term well-being. Doing them will make you happy and fulfilled.

The third lesson is to always remember to see obstacles and adversity as opportunities for you to get stronger, smarter, and better. There was once a king who decided to do a little experiment. He had a giant boulder secretly put right in the middle of the road in the middle of the night when no one was watching. He then hid near the boulder to see who, if anyone, would try to move it out of the way. First came some wealthy merchants walking by. They walked out around the boulder, complaining the whole time that the king hasn't been doing his job maintaining the roads very well. Next came a farmer. He walked by heading home with his arms full of food for his family. When he noticed the boulder he put his groceries down and attempted to move it. It was pretty difficult. It took him a while. He had to use a lever, but he finally got it to move off the road and out of the way. He saw it as a good deed and as a challenge, and he eventually succeeded.

After the farmer gathered up his groceries to carry on home, he noticed a bag lying in the middle of the road just where the boulder once had been. He opened the bag to find that it was stuffed full of gold coins along with a letter from the king saying that the bag of gold was a reward for the farmer to keep because he had taken the time and the energy to move the boulder out of the road for the convenience of others who would be traveling the road in the future. The farmer in this story knew that every obstacle you face offers an opportunity to improve. If you're able to push through moments that are challenging, you'll end up being much better off than you were before you started trying to overcome that challenge. The story also teaches a lesson of personal responsibility. If you see a job ahead of you, don't leave it for the next person to do; rather, step up and get the job done yourself and thereby help the people who will come after you. We must embrace our challenges in order to improve ourselves, and we must improve ourselves or we are missing the whole point of our mortal experience. Furthermore, we should always be actively engaged in a good cause of our own free will and, as the scripture says, bring about much righteousness.

The fourth lesson is to never rely on others to motivate you. Self-motivation is essential to your success in anything. You must have a burning desire in your own heart for your goal or you will never achieve that goal. A boy once asked a wise old man what the secret to success was. After listening to the boy's question, the wise man told the boy to meet him at the seaside in the morning and he would be given the answer there. In the morning, the wise man and the boy began walking toward the sea. They continued on into the water until it was close to covering their mouth and nose. At this time, the wise man quickly grabbed the young man and pushed him all the way under the water and held him there. As the young man struggled to get out, the wise man continued to push him further down. The boy struggled harder and harder as his panic increased. He struggled with all his might. Eventually the wise man pulled the boy's head up so he could get air.

The boy gasped as he inhaled a deep breath of air. The wise man said, "What were you fighting for when you were under the water?" The boy replied, "Air." "How much did you want it?" The boy said, "It was all I wanted." The wise man asked, "What else did you think about?" And the boy said, "Nothing else. All I thought about was getting some air." The wise man then said, "There you have the secret to success. When you want to gain success in something as much as you wanted air when you were under that water, you will get it. You will obtain it. That's the only secret." Success starts with the motivation to achieve something. If your motivation is weak, your results will also be weak. Think about what you desire the most in life and work towards getting it. Don't allow your environment or other people to influence the things that you truly want. Being able to motivate yourself is the most powerful skill you can build for yourself. Andrew Carnegie, the great steel magnate, said: "People who are unable to motivate themselves must be satisfied with mediocrity, no matter how smart they are or how impressive their other talents might be."

The fifth lesson is: be proactive, resilient, and tough-minded. One quote that I meditate on often is: "Show calm and self-possession at all times, but especially during hardship and disappointment. Adversity in all its forms provides the perfect setting for the exercise of self-discipline and the development of self-mastery. Furthermore, maintaining calm and unruffled exterior in the face of unpleasantness puts others at ease. Therefore, never show anger, ill temper, or vengefulness. Never whine, never complain, never try to justify yourself." I need to meditate on this quote often because it is such a difficult thing to control your own emotions, but nothing will set you apart in a positive way faster than to be a person who can be calm in the midst of the storms of life. And nothing will make people lose confidence in you faster than when they hear you whining and complaining about every problem you have.

A wise man once faced a group of people who were complaining about the same issues over and over again. One day, instead of listening to the complaints, he told them a joke and everyone cracked up laughing. Then the man repeated the same joke. Only a few people smiled this time. Finally, the man repeated the joke a third time, but this time no one laughed or even smiled. Then the man smiled and said to the people, "You won't laugh at the same joke more than once. So what do you think you're getting from continuing to complain about the same problem over and over again?"

Elders and sisters, you're not going to get anywhere in life if you keep complaining about the same problem, but do nothing to fix it. Don't waste your time complaining, expecting other people to continue to react to your complaints. Instead, take action to make a change. In fact, I found that if I will look for a solution before I complain, that I will usually be able to fix the problem myself. And even if I have to talk with someone to get some help about the problem, I can explain the proactive steps I've already taken and offer other potential solutions. This creates a completely different relationship with the person you are seeking help from. People admire people who bring potential solutions when they come seeking help on a problem.

The sixth lesson is to remember happiness is not something you find. It is actually something you choose. There were 200 people attending a seminar on mental and physical health. At one point, the speaker told the group that they were going to do an activity. He gave each attendee one balloon and told them to write their name on it. Then the balloons were collected and moved into a very small room. The participants were then asked to go into the other room and were given exactly two minutes to find their balloon. Well, it was chaos. People were searching frantically for their balloon, pushing each other around, running into each other while they grabbed a balloon, looked at it, and evidently tossed it aside. At the end of the two minutes, no one had found the balloon that had their name on it.

Then the speaker asked the participants to go back in the room and just pick up one balloon at random, look at the name, and return it to its owner. Within just a couple of minutes, everyone had been reunited with their original balloon. The speaker then told the group, "This is what it's like when people are frantically searching for their own happiness in life. People push others aside to get the things that they want, that they believe will bring them happiness." However, our happiness actually lies in helping other people and working together as a team. You will get your happiness if you help other people find theirs. Helping others makes us happy because it gives us a sense of purpose. In fact, a study from the London School of Economics found that the more you help other people, the happier you will be. So remember to choose happiness by choosing to serve others in ways that make them better and stronger. That will really make you happy.

The seventh and final lesson I want to share with you on this podcast is the lesson best taught through this story. A carpenter who was nearing retirement at the end of his long career told his boss that he was ready to finish and spend the rest of his time with his wife and family. He would miss his work but he felt like it was time to spend time with the people who were the most important in his life. His boss understood but was saddened by this news as this carpenter had been a very good, skilled craftsman and employee for many years. He asked the carpenter if he could do him a favor and build just one more house. The carpenter reluctantly agreed even though he didn't really want to. His passion for building had faded to nothing. But he started on the house and while he was building this last house, he found that his work ethic also had faded and his efforts were pretty mediocre at best. He used inexpensive and inferior materials. He cut corners wherever he could. It was a poor way to finish a dedicated career that he had once had, but he was just tired of it.

When the carpenter was finished, his boss came to look at the house and he then gave the key to the carpenter and said, "This house is my gift to you for all of the hard work you have done for me over the years." Well, the carpenter was astonished. What a generous gift this was to receive from his boss. But if he'd only known when he was building a house for himself, he would have made a very different effort to create a very high quality home. Well, this same idea applies to how you and I build our lives. Every day that you wake up offers an opportunity for you to do your best work. Yet most people often do the bare minimums, cutting corners and slacking off. Then one day, that person is shocked to discover that all the corners cut and all the time wasted actually cost them the quality life that they could have had. Their lives aren't what they could have been. Their lives aren't what they hoped they had been. The house they had built to live in had a lot of flaws, a lot of things that weren't good due to the lack of effort and commitment in the building of it. However, at that point in life, you can't go back and rebuild it in just a day or two. So you're young now, elders and sisters. Remember your attitude and your choices now actually build the life you will live tomorrow and throughout eternity. So build well.

Elders and sisters, there is so much more that I would love to share with you, but time is running short. I want to close with a little bit of housekeeping. First of all, I have not been able to get on the missionary letter portal for three days and so have not been able to read any of your letters this week and probably won't be able to because I'll lose my access this evening. It would be very helpful to me because I want to read your letters. So it would be very helpful if you take the time to just copy the letter that you wrote to me this week from the missionary portal and then paste it into an email to my personal email account. The address is sfhughes@me.com. Again, that's sfhughes@me.com. That way I can get your letters and maybe even respond to you.

Secondly, at 4 p.m. today, Sister Hughes and I will be giving our phones and SIM cards to President and Sister Solancho. So any texts or calls you make to our numbers will go to them because those are their numbers from 4 p.m. today onwards. So just keep that in mind. Thirdly, thank you for your trust and your kindness. You are a truly remarkable group of young people and I have great expectations for you both in the rest of your missions and afterwards in the rest of your life. Sister Hughes and I truly love you and know that what we have been doing together in the Philippines Quezon City North Mission has been in accordance with the will of God and that he is pleased overall with our efforts. May that always be the case for us as we move forward into the next exciting season of our lives. May God bless each one of you, elders and sisters, now and throughout your lives is my prayer, and I know he will honor that as you are faithful and true. Good afternoon and God bless you.
